newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgarians hit hard as economy crumbles.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgarians hit hard as economy crumbles.

text.p: Gergana Nikolova says she won't even have bread to eat unless she sells one of the cheap religious icons from her outdoor market stall in a working class district of Sofia.

"If I don't sell something I'll starve," said the 65-year-old widow, a former Bulgarian government archivist living alone on a pension of 4,000 levs ($17) a month. "I don't even dream about meat or beans."
"My pension is enough only for two days," she said. "I haven't paid my heating bills for five months now. I can't imagine how I would be able to survive with these prices."
Life is hard for many of this east European country's nine million people and there are no signs of a quick change for the better.

A quarter of Bulgaria's banks are under central bank supervision and effectively closed, the lev has been devalued 230 percent against the dollar since January and inflation is more than 100 percent a year.

Unemployment officially is 12.5 percent and likely to go up another percentage point soon as the socialist-led government, filled with former communists, implements reforms, including shutting down or selling off dozens of loss-making state enterprises.

Nikolai Koichev, a Socialist member of parliament and head of the economic committee, says the reforms may placate the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which is withholding the release of a second $115 million tranche of a standby loan, but won't do much to put food on the table.
"By international standards, about 90 percent of Bulgarians are living in poverty," Koichev told Reuters.
"In the past the living standard has been guaranteed -- not at the level of the West -- but secure. Now there is great poverty in Bulgaria."

Last week, in a desperate bid to salvage the economy, the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) hiked its main interest rate to an all time high of 300 percent and put nine more of the country's 42 banks under its supervision, for a total of 14.
In a televised speech the same day, Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov announced plans to sell off half a dozen state enterprises by the end of the year in the hope of raising $1 billion.

Diplomats said the actions should go a long way to convince the IMF the government is serious about overhauling Bulgaria's heavily indebted economy, saddled with some $10 billion in foreign debt, 600 billion levs of internal debt and dozens of loss-making state enterprises.
But it seemed to do little to dampen a growing sense among Bulgarians that things are not working out.
"It seems the state has made a great mistake in its policy,"said Dr Ivan Marinov as he waited at a bus stop, holding a shopping bag full of car parts.

Marinov said he earns 12,000 levs ($52) a month as a physician and his wife also works. But he had just spent 40,000 levs ($174) on car parts, many imported, and had probably lost much of his savings because it was in one of the closed banks.
"Things are only getting worse," he said.
The leading Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) opposition party, which lost the 1994 parliamentary elections, sees an opportunity to turn the tables in an October presidential poll.
Alexander Boshkov, UDF vice chairman, said the socialists had acted out of panic when they raised interest rates and put the banks under supervision.
"It is absurd on the one hand to raise the interest rates in order to increase confidence in the banks and then declare nine savings banks bankrupt," he told Reuters.
He faulted the government's privatisation programme as a case of too little, too late.

"The ownership is still 95 percent in the hands of the state and the state is totally incapable of managing it," he said. "The government is totally corrupt -- it is more corrupt than a banana republic."
Koichev acknowledged that corruption undoubtedly existed and said some of the luxurious Mercedes saloon cars and BMWs around Sofia were financed by people making a living "on the black economy".

"As a politician and a lawmaker I am strongly determined to fight and take measures against the corruption," he said, adding that he thought that in the long term the government's economic plan would succeed.
"Probably after some time the country's economy will stabilise, but at a much lower level in comparison with the other European countries," he said.
For people like the widow Nikolova, living in the outer districts of Sofia where horsedrawn carts still haul goods and goats graze alongside yards piled high with junked cars, it could come too late.
"But not only I am in this situation," she said. "There are well-dressed people in Bulgaria, looking for bread in the garbage containers, people who have lost their jobs or were not able to find any.
"I can see things getting even worse in the future."
